At Templo Mayor, modern Mexico City seems to lift the surface of its streets to reveal what lies beneath. Beside the cathedral and Zócalo square, the stone foundations, stairways, and walls of an ancient temple complex remain visible. This was the main temple of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Mexica people, commonly known as the Aztecs.

Two sanctuaries dedicated to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli stood at the top of the main pyramid. The temple was expanded repeatedly, and the excavations reveal different stages of construction. Walk slowly through the site: among the surviving stonework, it is easier to imagine how the ancient ceremonial center gradually disappeared beneath the new city. Today, archaeological remains mark the site of the once-tall temple.

The Templo Mayor Museum complements the visit with finds from the complex. One of its principal exhibits is a stone disk depicting the goddess Coyolxauhqui. Sculptures and ritual offerings help explain the significance of the remains outside. History enthusiasts will find this a rewarding stop: afterward, the familiar streets around Zócalo can be seen in the context of the ancient city beneath them.

Tenorio Volcano National Park protects a natural area surrounding a volcanic massif in Costa Rica. Rainforest surrounds Río Celeste, a river known for the striking blue hue of its water. The main attractions are walks through the forest and along stretches of river where the color is particularly visible.

One of the park's best-known sights is the Río Celeste waterfall. At Los Teñideros, visitors can see where the water takes on its blue color. Walking these trails reveals the river among trees, at the cascade, and where its streams meet. Tenorio makes a worthwhile nature stop between other regions of Costa Rica.

In Teotitlán del Valle, visitors can watch how woven textiles take shape. Wooden looms stand in family workshops, alongside wool and finished pieces. The weaver gradually turns individual threads into a pattern. Seeing the process up close changes how you look at even a small rug hanging on a wall.

The village in the Oaxaca Valley is known for its Zapotec textile tradition. Artisans make wool rugs and other pieces, using natural pigments to create different shades. In a workshop, you can learn how colors are produced and patterns chosen. A conversation with a weaver reveals the family knowledge and hours of handwork behind each finished item.

Teotitlán is a rewarding stop for travelers interested in crafts who want to bring home something with a clear provenance. Visit a workshop, browse the local market, or explore the village's traditional cuisine. Arrangements for meeting artisans are confirmed when planning the trip. Choosing a piece feels especially meaningful after seeing the loom, the wool, and the hands that made it.

## Teotihuacan: "The Place Where the Gods Are Born"

The "ghost city" of Teotihuacan stands 40 km northeast of Mexico City, in the municipality of San Juan Teotihuacan. This ancient settlement dates back around two thousand years; the name is rendered in the source as "the place where the gods touch the earth" in the Aztec language. Today, Teotihuacan is a vast archaeological complex best known for the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon.

## Teotihuacan: An Ancient Ceremonial Complex

Teotihuacan is also translated as "the place where the gods are born." It was a ceremonial complex for many Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica. Ancient Teotihuacan is one of Mexico's most visited archaeological sites. The precise time of the first settlements and the reasons its inhabitants abandoned the city are still unknown. These "stone treasures of history," built from enormous blocks, follow an intricate system whose meaning is not fully understood. The scale is impressive: the Pyramid of the Sun is described as the third-largest pyramid in the world.
